body:
The economic and political background

The Navnirman Movement was a major protest movement in Gujarat in 1974. It emerged during a period of rising prices, shortages of essential commodities and public dissatisfaction with corruption in government.

Across India, the early 1970s were marked by inflation and economic hardship. Higher prices of foodgrains, cooking oil and other necessities directly affected household expenditure and students' living costs. In Gujarat, complaints about price increases became linked with wider criticism of the state government.

From student agitation to a statewide movement

The agitation became a statewide movement in January 1974 with students protesting rising costs and corruption; student protests over increased mess charges had begun in December 1973. Student unrest in Ahmedabad, including protests associated with increased hostel and mess expenses, helped give the agitation momentum.

The protest subsequently spread beyond educational institutions. Wider sections of the public and major opposition parties joined it. The movement came to be known as Navnirman, meaning reconstruction or renewal, because its supporters demanded political change and a government they considered more accountable.

Resignation of Chimanbhai Patel

Chimanbhai Patel, who had become Gujarat's Chief Minister on 17 July 1973, was in office when the agitation intensified.

On 9 February 1974, he resigned. President's Rule was imposed in Gujarat on the same date. The Legislative Assembly was initially suspended and subsequently dissolved on 15 March 1974.

President's Rule is a constitutional arrangement under Article 356 in which a state comes under Union administration when its government cannot be carried on in accordance with the Constitution. It is imposed by a presidential proclamation and requires approval by each House of Parliament by a simple majority of members present and voting, normally within 2 months. During such a period, there is no elected state council of ministers exercising the normal powers of government.

The Chief Minister's resignation, the imposition of President's Rule and the dissolution of the Assembly were distinct events. They did not all occur on the same date.

The 1975 election and its significance

The opposition demanded fresh elections. Morarji Desai, a prominent Congress (O) leader, announced an indefinite fast unless elections were held. The continuing pressure contributed to the decision to hold Assembly elections in June 1975.

The Congress was defeated in that election. A government headed by Babubhai Jashbhai Patel, associated with the Janata Morcha, took office on 18 June 1975. The sequence shows how an agitation that began over everyday economic grievances developed into a major change in state politics.

Navnirman, the Bihar Movement and the Emergency

Two related events in national political history must be distinguished from Gujarat's Navnirman Movement.

  • Bihar Movement, 1974: Student protests in Bihar began in March 1974 and later came under the leadership of Jayaprakash Narayan, who called for wider political and social change.
  • National Emergency, 1975: A national Emergency was proclaimed on 25 June 1975. This happened after the June 1975 Gujarat Assembly election.

These movements formed part of a wider period of political unrest, but they had different immediate locations, leadership patterns and constitutional outcomes. Gujarat's President's Rule began in February 1974; the national Emergency began in June 1975.

Prelims focus

  • Student protests began in December 1973; Navnirman became a statewide movement in January 1974.
  • Its immediate grievances included rising prices and corruption.
  • Chimanbhai Patel resigned on 9 February 1974.
  • President's Rule began on 9 February 1974; the Assembly was dissolved on 15 March 1974.
  • Congress was defeated in the June 1975 Gujarat Assembly election.
  • Babubhai J. Patel took office on 18 June 1975.
  • Trap: Navnirman in Gujarat was not the Bihar Movement led by Jayaprakash Narayan, and it was not the national Emergency of 25 June 1975.

[NCERT, Class 12, Politics in India since Independence, Chapter 6, 'The Crisis of Democratic Order,' printed pp. 103–104 and 108–109; Lok Sabha Secretariat, President's Rule in States and Union Territories, 9th edition, January 2016, Gujarat entry, printed p. 14; Lok Sabha Secretariat, Journal of Parliamentary Information, July–September 1974, Gujarat section on the resignation of the ministry and President's Rule; Indian Express, coverage of the Navnirman Movement's 1974 chronology, consulted 23 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Students gather peacefully outside an Ahmedabad college in January 1974 to protest rising hostel and food costs.
Gujarat’s sequence from student protests to a new Chief Minister, with resignation, dissolution and elections dated separately from the later national Emergency.
pictures.caption: Navnirman, President's Rule, dissolution and fresh elections were separate stages.

title: The Navnirman Movement of 1974: Causes and Political Consequences

body:
Why the new state developed its own institutions

After its formation in 1960, Gujarat had to organise administration, economic development and local self-government. Several early laws and institutions addressed different needs. Land-ceiling legislation concerned agricultural holdings, industrial development concerned organised industrial infrastructure, and Panchayati Raj concerned local government in rural areas.

These measures should be distinguished by their purposes rather than treated as parts of one programme.

Agricultural land-ceiling legislation

The Gujarat Agricultural Lands Ceiling Act, 1960 provided for limits on the agricultural land that could be held and for the acquisition and disposal of surplus agricultural land. Its purpose was to regulate large holdings and provide a legal mechanism for dealing with land above the prescribed ceiling.

An important date distinction arises from the official text: although the law's short title contains 1960, it appears as Gujarat Act 27 of 1961, dated 15 June 1961.

A land ceiling is the maximum permitted holding determined under the applicable legal provisions. Land above that limit can be identified as surplus and dealt with according to the Act. The ceiling is not necessarily one identical acreage figure for every type of land; the law provides for differences in land classification and other conditions.

Industrial development and GIDC

The Gujarat Industrial Development Act, 1962 provided for the organisation of industrial areas and estates. The Gujarat Industrial Development Corporation (GIDC) was established in 1962 to promote industrial development through planned industrial infrastructure.

Its functions included identifying suitable land, developing industrial areas, allotting plots and providing infrastructure such as roads, water supply and other facilities needed by industrial units.

GIDC is an industrial development institution; it is not a Panchayat or an agricultural land-ceiling authority.

The beginning of Panchayati Raj in Gujarat

Panchayati Raj refers to institutions of rural local self-government. Following the recommendations associated with the Balwantrai Mehta Committee, Gujarat adopted the Gujarat Panchayats Act, 1961. The three-tier Panchayati Raj arrangement began functioning in the state on 1 April 1963.

The three levels are:

  • Village Panchayat: local self-government at the village level.
  • Taluka Panchayat: an intermediate institution covering the taluka level.
  • District Panchayat: a district-level rural local-government institution.

These are territorial levels of local government. They are not three different departments of the state secretariat.

The 1993 Panchayats Act

The 73rd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1992, which came into force on 24 April 1993, gave Panchayati Raj institutions a constitutional framework through Part IX of the Constitution.

Gujarat subsequently enacted the Gujarat Panchayats Act, 1993, Gujarat Act 18 of 1993, assented to on 26 August 1993. It established provisions for village, taluka and district panchayats and replaced the earlier 1961 legislation; the State Government could notify different commencement dates, while existing rights, liabilities and pending proceedings were preserved.

The Act also recognises the Gram Sabha, consisting of persons registered in the electoral rolls relating to the village. The Gram Sabha is not an additional fourth tier of Panchayati Raj; it is the village-level body of registered voters.

Prelims focus

  • Gujarat Agricultural Lands Ceiling Act, 1960: Gujarat Act 27 of 1961.
  • Gujarat Industrial Development Act: 1962.
  • GIDC was established in 1962.
  • Gujarat Panchayats Act: 1961; three-tier Panchayati Raj functioning from 1 April 1963.
  • 73rd Constitutional Amendment: 1992; effective from 24 April 1993.
  • Gujarat Panchayats Act, 1993: Gujarat Act 18 of 1993.
  • Trap: The Gram Sabha is not a fourth tier of Panchayati Raj.

[Government of Gujarat, Gujarat Agricultural Lands Ceiling Act, 1960, Gujarat Act 27 of 1961, preamble and sections 1, 5, 6, 21 and 29, official text modified up to 31 May 2012; Government of Gujarat, Gujarat Industrial Development Act, 1962, Gujarat Act 23 of 1962, preamble and sections 3 and 13; Gujarat Industrial Development Corporation, official FAQ, 'What is GIDC?' and 'What are the functions/activities undertaken by GIDC?', consulted 23 November 2026; Government of Gujarat, Tribal Development Department, Annual Report on the Administration of Scheduled Areas 2019–20, Chapter IV, section 4.1.2; Government of Gujarat, Gujarat Panchayats Act, 1993, sections 3, 4 and 276, official consolidated text modified up to 31 May 2017.]

pictures.alt: Gujarat has district, taluka and village Panchayat tiers; Gram Sabha is the assembly of registered village voters, not a fourth tier.
pictures.caption: The three Panchayati Raj tiers are village, taluka and district.

pictures.alt: Three parallel comparisons connect Gujarat’s land, industry and Panchayat laws to their distinct purposes, with key dates.
pictures.caption: Land regulation, industrial development and rural self-government served different purposes.

title: Major State Reforms: Land, Industry and Panchayati Raj

body:
How the Chief Minister's office fits into state government

The Chief Minister heads the elected government of a state. The Governor appoints the Chief Minister, who normally leads a party or coalition commanding the confidence of the Legislative Assembly. The Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to the Assembly.

A change of Chief Minister does not change the state's formation date or constitutional identity. Moreover, there can be periods of President's Rule between elected ministries, so the historical sequence of Chief Ministers is not necessarily uninterrupted.

From Jivraj Mehta to Chimanbhai Patel

PeriodChief Minister or administrationHistorical distinction
1 May 1960–19 September 1963Dr. Jivraj Narayan MehtaFirst Chief Minister of Gujarat
19 September 1963–19 September 1965Balwantrai MehtaSecond Chief Minister
19 September 1965–12 May 1971Hitendra DesaiThird Chief Minister
13 May 1971–17 March 1972President's RuleNo elected ministry in office
17 March 1972–17 July 1973Ghanshyam OzaChief Minister before Chimanbhai Patel
17 July 1973–9 February 1974Chimanbhai PatelResigned during Navnirman agitation
9 February 1974–18 June 1975President's RulePeriod between Navnirman and new ministry
From 18 June 1975Babubhai Jashbhai PatelHeaded government after Congress defeat

Important distinctions between leaders and events

Dr. Jivraj Mehta was Gujarat's first Chief Minister from its formation. His tenure established the initial elected administration of the state. Balwantrai Mehta succeeded him in 1963. His name is also associated with the earlier Balwantrai Mehta Committee, whose recommendations influenced Panchayati Raj. The committee's work and his tenure as Gujarat's Chief Minister belong to different stages of history.

Hitendra Desai became Chief Minister in 1965. The first period of President's Rule in Gujarat began on 13 May 1971, after his ministry ended. The state returned to elected government under Ghanshyam Oza in March 1972.

Chimanbhai Patel assumed office in July 1973. His first tenure ended during the Navnirman Movement in February 1974. The next elected ministry began only in June 1975, under Babubhai J. Patel.

The 1971 President's Rule and the 1974 President's Rule were separate periods. The 1974 proclamation followed the Navnirman agitation; the earlier one did not.

Prelims focus

  • First Chief Minister: Dr. Jivraj Narayan Mehta, from 1 May 1960.
  • Second Chief Minister: Balwantrai Mehta, from September 1963.
  • Third Chief Minister: Hitendra Desai, from September 1965.
  • First President's Rule in Gujarat: 13 May 1971.
  • Ghanshyam Oza became Chief Minister in March 1972.
  • Chimanbhai Patel resigned on 9 February 1974.
  • Babubhai J. Patel became Chief Minister on 18 June 1975.
  • Trap: A period of President's Rule is not counted as a Chief Minister's tenure.

[Indian Institute of Management Ahmedabad Archives, 'Dr. Jivraj N. Mehta,' biographical record; Lok Sabha Secretariat, President's Rule in States and Union Territories, 9th edition, January 2016, Gujarat entry, printed p. 14; Gujarat chief-minister historical tenure compilation, All Gujarat News, 27 July 2022; NCERT, Class 12, Politics in India since Independence, Chapter 6, 'The Crisis of Democratic Order,' printed p. 104; Government of Gujarat, Tribal Development Department, Annual Report on the Administration of Scheduled Areas 2019–20, Chapter IV, section 4.1.2.]
